job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Emeka Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I graduated in finance from Delmont University this summer. I live in a rented room in my uncle Chidi's house in the port city of Karsby, because the rest of my family is a long train ride away. My day starts with morning prayers, then I look at the job boards and send out five or six applications. In the afternoons I help my uncle with the invoices for his freight brokerage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest part is the waiting. I've sent about forty-five applications and I've had three interviews, but nobody has said yes. What I like is the discipline of finance: at my internship at Orlen Freight, a transport firm, I checked supplier invoices against deliveries, and I found a double payment of 3,200 that saved them real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's what a sensible person would expect. New things get oversold. I'd tell my uncle that hard work and good timing still win, and that the market will work it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still in the same hole. I have a good degree, some debt and about six weeks of savings. My family has helped me with the rent, and I don't want to rely on it for long. AI doing a bit of routine work doesn't change the number of graduate jobs, which is the real problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, forty or fifty applications more, and I'd widen it to logistics and transport firms, since I know that world through my father and Orlen. I'd keep helping my uncle for a small fee. I'd keep using AI now and then, mostly to tidy my emails and check my Excel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I'm anxious about money, though not about AI, and I pray about it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your father runs a transport business. How does he see your job search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father said, 'Son, a good invoice clerk is more use than a clever one who never shows up.' He thinks the job search is like a long haul, where you keep your wheels turning. I'd agree with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your uncle's brokerage teach you about how the market works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learned that the market pays people who solve a problem, not people with a certificate. My uncle gets paid because he finds a truck when a customer's stuck. I want to be the person who makes that kind of problem go away on the finance side.

say: I'd say new things get oversold, and **hard work and timing** still win.
I'd tell my uncle the **market will work it** out.
think: I'm in the **same hole** as before: good degree, some debt and about six weeks of savings.
AI doing routine work doesn't change the **number of graduate jobs**.
do: Send **forty or fifty more** applications, widening to logistics and transport firms.
Help my uncle with **freight invoices** for a small fee.
Use AI **now and then** to tidy emails and check Excel.
feel: It feels **steady**, with money worries that I take to prayer.
S0.quote: I learned that the market pays people who solve a problem, not people with a certificate.
fieldNote: Emeka's worry is **money and jobs**, not AI, and he says so clearly.
He draws on **his father's and uncle's** transport world as a second place to look.
His faith is a **steadying habit**, not a plan.

steps.text: Send fifty applications to logistics and transport firms
Do the freight invoices for my uncle for a fee
Use AI to proofread emails and check Excel formulas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, so people should work harder and learn to use the new tools sensibly. I'd say that government should not hand out money for ever, but should back training and apprenticeships that lead to a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the invoice checking I did at Orlen is exactly what software does. Matching delivery notes to payments is boring and quick for a machine, so entry-level roles in finance will shrink. I'd need to move up a level to avoid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI properly, every week, for reconciliations and reports, and ask my uncle if I can run his invoices through it as a trial. I'd apply to logistics firms and look for apprenticeship-style schemes. I'd do an evening course in data analysis, paid for by my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels challenging but fair. I don't blame anyone, but I do feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your own tasks at Orlen would be easiest for software to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The invoice matching and payment checks, easily. The part that's harder is a call with a driver who says the load was damaged, and deciding who pays. That needs judgement and a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to try a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wait until two people I trust are using it, then I try it. That's how I decide. With the AI tools my uncle's accountant started using, I saw the results in a month, and then I tried it myself.

say: I'd say **people should learn the** tools sensibly, and government should back training that leads to a job.
think: The invoice checking I did is **what software does**, so entry finance roles will shrink.
I'd need to **move up a level** to avoid it.
do: Use AI **every week** for reconciliations and reports.
Run my uncle's **invoices through it** as a trial.
Take an **evening data course** paid for from savings.
feel: It feels **challenging but fair**, and I feel the clock.
S1.quote: I wait until two people I trust are using it, then I try it. That's how I decide.
fieldNote: Emeka shows **steady adaptability**: waits for proof from trusted people, then acts.
He wants **training linked to jobs**, consistent with his traditional outlook.
He sees the **human judgement** in disputes as safe for now.

steps.text: Use AI weekly for reconciliations and reports
Run my uncle's invoices through AI as a trial
Apply to logistics firms with training schemes
Take an evening data analysis course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough. Governments and businesses must tell families clearly what is coming, and communities like my church should look after those who fall behind. I'd say we shouldn't panic, but we shouldn't sleep either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be afraid. If AI does all thinking work in two years, the finance route I trained for is mostly shut. I'd be competing with software and thousands of other graduates, all in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my father and uncle in the first week. I'd put everything into work that still needs a person: dispatch, customs paperwork, vehicle inspections, and I'd ask my father about a place in his firm. I'd cut my spending to the basics and save every spare pound, and I'd keep praying and keep my church group close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a storm warning with only two days to board up the windows. I'd be tense, but I'd be busy, and busy helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first, and what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father first, because he built the business and knows what trucks and customers need. I'd ask my father whether the firm needs a person who can run the numbers and keep the paperwork human, and whether it can survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the two-year warning change the way you think about your father's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His trucks are hands-on, so the robots take about three years longer than the office AI. But dispatch and invoicing are desk work, so those would go in 2028, and he'd probably need fewer office staff. I'd tell him to start moving some of the work now.

say: I'd say two years is **not enough**, and families must be told clearly what's coming.
I'd say churches should **look after those** who fall behind.
think: If AI does all thinking work, the **finance route is mostly** shut.
I'd compete with software and **thousands of graduates** in the same year.
do: Talk to my **father and uncle** in the first week.
Move to **work that still needs** a person: dispatch, customs paperwork and inspections.
**Cut spending** to the basics and keep my church group close.
feel: It feels like a **storm warning** with two days to board up the windows.
S2.quote: I'd ask my father whether the firm needs a person who can run the numbers and keep the paperwork human
fieldNote: Emeka's plan **turns to family and** faith, then the family firm, before anything abstract.
He sees that **dispatch and invoicing** at his father's firm would go on the stated date.
Even with a plan, he **expects to lose the** finance route, so alarmed.

steps.text: Talk to my father about a place in his firm
Apply for dispatch and customs paperwork jobs
Cut spending to rent, food and phone
Advise my father to move invoicing to AI now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a sensible country to prepare. We should train young people, support small firms and tell people straight what's coming, and I'd say this to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but with a plan. I'd have time to get a first job, move up one level, pay off my debt and be useful to a firm that is changing. I'd also have time for a family plan, which matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in logistics finance within the year, save half my pay, and learn the AI tools they use. I'd propose to my girlfriend Ada in two years, if we're both settled. I'd keep supporting my uncle and keep going to church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long road with a hard bend near the end. I'd keep my eyes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two years doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give me time to marry, to save or to learn. Five years does, and the hands-on side of my father's business gives us three extra years to move the office side across.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you advise your father about the firm over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to bring in AI for the invoicing and dispatch first, but keep his best drivers and his customer relationships. In five years, we'd have a smaller office and the same loyal drivers.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **sensible country** to prepare.
I'd say we must **tell people straight** what's coming.
think: I'd be anxious but with a plan: **first job**, move up a level, pay off my debt.
I'd also have time for a **family plan**.
do: Get a **first logistics finance job** within the year and save half my pay.
Learn the **AI tools** that firm uses.
Plan to **propose to Ada** in two years if we're both settled.
feel: It feels like a **long road** with a hard bend near the end.
S3.quote: In five years, we'd have a smaller office and the same loyal drivers.
fieldNote: Five years lets Emeka plan **marriage, savings and a** job in order.
He advises his father to **automate the office first** and keep the drivers.
His mood falls to anxious because he sees **a workable sequence**.

steps.text: Get a first job in logistics finance
Save half of every pay cheque
Propose to Ada within two years
Help move my father's invoicing onto AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it right. We should rebuild apprenticeships, keep families together and let people earn through work, and I'd say that this is a gift, not a threat, if we use it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel fairly settled. In ten years I could be married, qualified, perhaps a manager and able to help my father's firm change gently. I'd still worry about the last stretch, but I'd be well placed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a good job, qualify, save and start learning the tools properly. I'd buy a small house in Karsby by 30, and I'd put money aside for children's school fees. I'd probably go back and help my father run the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long season. I'd work, pray and wait for the harvest, and I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you want to have built by the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a house, a family and a good name at work. If I've got those, then AGI is a thing I meet as a man with something to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still pick finance if you started again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still finance, but with logistics, because it's something I understand. Money and trucks both move, and someone has to be honest about where they go.

I'd call it a **gift, not a threat**.
think: In ten years I could be **married and qualified**, perhaps a manager.
I'd still worry about the **last stretch**.

fieldNote: Emeka's ten-year view is **family-centred**: house, children and a good name.

steps.text: Get a good job and qualify as an accountant
Buy a small house in Karsby by age 30
Learn AI tools properly alongside work
Plan to help my father run the firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because I'd have no time to settle, marry or save. What would help is apprenticeships that lead to a job, plain information from leaders, and communities that look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that a person is more than a CV, and we want to earn our place rather than be given it. I'd like whoever reads this to know that those of us from families with small firms have something to offer, and that we want to earn our place rather than be given it.

headlineQuote: A person is more than a CV, and we want to earn our place rather than be given it.
portrait: Emeka is a 23-year-old **finance graduate** renting a room at his uncle's house in Karsby, with no offer.
He has some debt, about **six weeks of savings**, and uses AI now and then.
He is traditional, religious and family-minded, wants **apprenticeships** and work over handouts, and trusts people he knows.
His moods run from anxious to alarmed at two years, and he looks to his **father's transport firm** as a second path.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because there'd be no time to settle, marry or save.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships leading to jobs**, plain information from leaders and communities that look after each other would help.
